standard_text: Define slope as vertical change for each unit of horizontal change, and apply that a constant rate of change or constant slope describes a linear function. Identify and describe situations with constant or varying rates of change.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to define slope as vertical change for each unit of horizontal change and to recognize that a constant rate of change describes a linear function. The on-grade skills build from naming the vertical and horizontal parts of a slope, to checking a table for equal step-by-step changes, to sorting real situations into constant amounts versus percents and doublings, and finally to interpreting a given slope in context. Students who stall here usually cannot find a per-one rate or move confidently on a coordinate grid. Intervention should rebuild equal-groups multiplication and first-quadrant plotting from the elementary grades, then the grade six skills of finding a unit rate and graphing a relationship from a table, and only then return to slope and constant rates.

steps.rationale: The definitional entry move: name slope as vertical change over horizontal change and identify which number is which. Everything else depends on reading a slope correctly.
From a table, decide constant vs varying by checking whether the step-by-step changes are equal. This is where the 'increasing means constant' misconception must be settled.
Move from tables to described situations: recognize the one with a constant amount per unit (linear) among percent/multiplicative distractors.
The mirror of S3: pick out the situation whose amount of change varies (percent, doubling, halving), separating a varying rate from a merely changing total.
Apply the definition in context: read a given slope as 'rises TOP for every BOTTOM across,' the meaning the At-proficiency items demand.
The Above-proficiency synthesis: compute segment rates from a table whose rate shifts, and justify why one linear function cannot model it.

skills.name: Plot and name points in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid

prerequisite_skill.description: Given an ordered pair, move across first and then up from zero to plot the point, and name a plotted point as an ordered pair.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (3, 5), how far do you go across and how far do you go up?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is a set of directions from the corner of the grid: across first, then up. Watch: to plot (3, 5), I start at 0, walk 3 spaces across, then climb 5 spaces up, and mark the point. The first number is always the across number and the second is always the up number, so (3, 5) and (5, 3) land in different places. To name a point already on the grid, I read it the same way: how far across, then how far up.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair, going up first and across second
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going up 3 and across 5, landing at the point (5, 3)
canonical_error.why: The student treats the two numbers as interchangeable. The order carries meaning: the first number is always the across distance and the second is always the up distance.

skills.item_template: An ordered pair to plot or a plotted point to name, first quadrant only, whole numbers to 10. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot the point (3, 5), how far do you go across and how far up?
A point is 4 across and 2 up from 0. Write its ordered pair.
In the ordered pair (6, 1), which number tells how far across?
In the ordered pair (5, 3), which number tells how far up?
A point sits 0 across and 7 up. Write its ordered pair.
Which point is farther up: (2, 8) or (8, 2)?
Write the ordered pair for the corner of the grid where you start.
Do (4, 9) and (9, 4) name the same point?
sample_items.answer: No, the across and up distances are switched

redirect_script.stop: Which number did you use first, and which direction did it send you?
redirect_script.prompt: The first number is the across number and the second is the up number, every time. Start at 0, walk across first, then climb up. Say it as you move: across, then up.
redirect_script.praise: You went across first and up second, so the point landed exactly where the pair says.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers in parentheses that locate a point: the first tells how far across, the second how far up.
A grid of squares with a horizontal axis and a vertical axis that meet at 0, used to locate points.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 coordinate grids with a floor grid or taped axes: walk across first, then up, starting from 0.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid from 0 to 10 on both axes. Put your pencil on 0.
To plot (3, 5), which number sends you across and which sends you up?
Across first: count 3 spaces to the right. Then up: count 5 spaces. Mark the point. The pair (3, 5) means 3 across and 5 up, in that order.
If a student climbs 3 and walks 5, plot both points and compare: (3, 5) and (5, 3) are different places, so the order matters.
Your turn: plot (6, 2), then tell me the ordered pair for a point 1 across and 8 up.

skills.name: Multiply and divide with equal groups

prerequisite_skill.description: Solve equal-groups problems: find a total from equal groups, and share a total into equal groups.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: 18 stickers are shared equally among 3 friends. How many stickers does each friend get?

skills.i_do_script: Equal groups means every group holds the same amount. Watch: 4 boxes hold 5 pencils each. I draw 4 circles with 5 dots in each and count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. So 4 x 5 = 20 pencils. Division undoes it: if 18 stickers are shared equally among 3 friends, I deal them out one at a time into 3 circles until they are gone, and each circle holds 6. Same size in every group, that is what makes multiplying and dividing work.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the number of groups and the group size instead of multiplying
canonical_error.example: For 4 boxes of 5 pencils, answers 9 because 4 + 5 = 9
canonical_error.why: The student combines the two numbers instead of repeating the group. The 4 counts how many groups there are and the 5 counts what is inside each one, so the total is 5 taken 4 times, not 4 plus 5.

skills.item_template: An equal-groups story or a bare fact within the times tables (products to 40). Student multiplies to find a total or divides to share equally. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: 4 boxes hold 5 pencils each. How many pencils in all?
18 stickers are shared equally among 3 friends. How many does each friend get?
There are 5 shelves with 7 books on each shelf. How many books in all?
20 apples are packed 4 to a bag. How many bags?

redirect_script.stop: How many groups are there, and how many are inside each group?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the groups: one circle for each group, the same number of dots in every circle. The total is the group size counted once for every group, so multiply. To share, deal the total into the circles evenly.
redirect_script.praise: You made equal groups and counted them, that is exactly what multiplication means.

vocabulary.definition: Groups that all hold the same amount.
Share a total into equal groups, or find how many equal groups fit inside a total.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 equal groups with counters: build the groups, then count the total.

worked_example_script.text: Draw 4 circles. Put 5 dots in each circle.
How many groups? How many in each group? How can we count the total quickly?
Count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. So 4 groups of 5 is 4 x 5 = 20. Every circle holds the same amount, so skip counting works.
If a student says 9, point at the picture: does 4 + 5 count all these dots? The 4 tells how many circles, not how many dots.
Your turn: 3 bags hold 6 marbles each. Draw the groups and find the total.

skills.name: Find a unit rate from a real-world ratio situation

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a rate like 120 miles in 3 hours, divide to find the amount for 1 unit.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A car travels 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. How many miles is that per hour?

skills.i_do_script: A unit rate tells how much for exactly 1: 1 hour, 1 ticket, 1 pound. Watch: a car goes 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. I split the 120 miles evenly across the 3 hours, 120 divided by 3 is 40, so the unit rate is 40 miles per hour. The amount being measured goes on top and the 1-unit quantity goes on the bottom, because the question is miles for each 1 hour. On a double number line, 3 hours sits under 120 miles, and cutting both into 3 equal parts puts 1 hour under 40 miles.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides in the wrong order, computing units per amount instead of amount per unit
canonical_error.example: For 120 miles in 3 hours, computes 3 / 120 = 0.025 instead of 120 / 3 = 40
canonical_error.why: The student divides without deciding which quantity should become 1. Miles per hour means miles for each 1 hour, so the miles get split by the hours. Dividing the other way answers a different question, hours per mile.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate with clean numbers (two quantities, one to be scaled to 1). Student divides to find the unit rate and labels it. Numeric or short response; occasional MC.

sample_items.stem: A car travels 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. What is its speed in miles per hour?
A printer prints 90 pages in 5 minutes. How many pages per minute?
5 tickets cost $45. What is the price per ticket?
A tank drains 48 gallons in 4 minutes. What is the unit rate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 44 comes from subtracting 48 - 4; 192 from multiplying 48 x 4; 1/12 from dividing 4 / 48 (units per amount). Only 48 / 4 = 12 gives gallons for each 1 minute.

sample_items.stem: A runner covers 6 miles in 2 hours. How many miles per hour?
A recipe uses 10 cups of flour for 4 loaves. How many cups per loaf?
Mia types 150 words in 3 minutes. How many words per minute?
4 pounds of apples cost $6. What is the cost per pound?
sample_items.distractor_logic: $2.00 comes from rounding or from 6 - 4; $24.00 from multiplying 6 x 4; $0.67 from dividing 4 / 6 (pounds per dollar). Only 6 / 4 = 1.50 gives dollars for each 1 pound.

redirect_script.prompt: Say the rate out loud: miles PER HOUR means miles for each 1 hour. Split the miles evenly across the hours, so the miles get divided by the hours. If your answer is a tiny decimal when you expected a real speed, you divided the wrong way.
redirect_script.praise: You divided the amount by the number of units, so your answer tells what happens in exactly 1.

vocabulary.definition: The amount for exactly 1 of the other quantity, like miles for 1 hour or dollars for 1 pound.
For each 1. Miles per hour means miles for each 1 hour.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a double number line: hours on the bottom marked 0 to 3, miles on top marked 0 to 120, with 3 lined up under 120.
If the car covers 120 miles in 3 equal hours, how do we find what it covers in just 1 hour?
Cut both lines into 3 equal parts. Each hour of driving lines up with 120 / 3 = 40 miles. The unit rate is 40 miles per hour.
If a student computes 3 / 120, ask what the answer should describe: miles for 1 hour, or hours for 1 mile? The double number line shows 1 hour sitting under 40.
Your turn: a faucet fills 36 liters in 4 minutes. Draw the double number line and find the liters per minute.

practice_problems.stem: A bike rider covers 10 miles in 2 hours. How many miles per hour?
practice_problems.answer: 5 miles per hour

practice_problems.stem: 3 pounds of bananas cost $12. What is the price per pound?
practice_problems.answer: $4 per pound

practice_problems.stem: A student reads 84 pages in 4 days. How many pages per day?
practice_problems.answer: 21 pages per day

practice_problems.stem: A hose fills 18 liters in 4 minutes. How many liters per minute?
practice_problems.answer: 4.5 liters per minute

practice_problems.stem: 5 pens cost $7.50. What is the cost per pen?
practice_problems.answer: $1.50 per pen

practice_problems.stem: A swimmer completes 9 laps in 6 minutes. How many laps per minute?
practice_problems.answer: 1.5 laps per minute

practice_problems.stem: Which is faster: 90 miles in 2 hours, or 120 miles in 3 hours? Show the unit rates.
practice_problems.answer: 90 / 2 = 45 mph and 120 / 3 = 40 mph, so 90 miles in 2 hours is faster.

practice_problems.stem: Leo found the unit rate for 60 miles in 4 hours. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Leo divided the hours by the miles, which gives hours per mile. Miles per hour means miles for each 1 hour: 60 / 4 = 15 miles per hour.

activities.title: Deal Out the Miles
materials: Index cards labeled Hour 1, Hour 2, Hour 3, Hour 4
activities.instructions:
1. Pose: a car goes 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. Lay out 3 hour cards.
2. Deal 120 (as 12 ten-blocks) evenly onto the hour cards until they are gone.
3. Count one card: 40 miles. Say the sentence: 40 miles for each 1 hour.
4. Write the matching division 120 / 3 = 40 next to the cards.
5. Repeat with 90 pages in 5 minutes and $45 for 5 tickets. Each time, deal first, then write the division.

activities.title: Rate Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per situation, one card per unit rate
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each situation card, like 120 miles in 3 hours, to its unit-rate card, like 40 miles per hour.
3. To claim a match, say the division out loud: 120 divided by 3 is 40.
4. Two decoy cards divide the wrong way; set them aside and explain what question they actually answer.

decoys: 120 miles in 3 hours = 0.025 miles per hour

strategy_links.why: Dealing counters onto hour cards and reading a double number line make 'amount for each 1' concrete before the division rule is named.
The wrong-way division is a stable, predictable error; finding and fixing it in worked examples confronts it directly.
Thinking aloud 'which quantity becomes 1?' makes the invisible setup decision audible and checkable.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity should become 1 in this problem?
Say the rate as 'blank for each 1 blank.' What goes in the blanks?
What division matches dealing 120 miles onto 3 hour cards?
Does your answer make sense as a real speed or price?
How would the answer change if the question asked for hours per mile instead?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the small number by the large one and gets a tiny decimal.
misconception_redirects.say: Read the question again: miles per hour means miles for each 1 hour. Deal the miles onto the hours. Which number gets split?
misconception_redirects.praise: You split the amount across the units, so the answer tells what 1 unit gets.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student subtracts or multiplies the two quantities instead of dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: A rate shares the amount evenly across the units. Sharing evenly is division. Deal it out with counters and watch what operation you are doing.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the dealing to division, that is what a rate is.

quick_checks.prompt: 80 miles in 4 hours. Miles per hour?
quick_checks.look_for: 20 miles per hour, from 80 / 4, not 0.05 from 4 / 80.
$6 per ticket, with the dollars divided by the ticket count and the label included.

worked_solution.stem: A car travels 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. Find its speed in miles per hour.

steps.math: unit rate = miles for each 1 hour
steps.annotation: Decide which quantity becomes 1: the hours.
Split the 120 miles evenly across the 3 hours.
Each hour carries 40 miles.
Label the answer as amount per 1 unit.

faded_example.stem: A train travels 150 miles in 5 hours at a steady speed. Find its speed in miles per hour.

steps.math: unit rate = miles for each 1 hour
steps.annotation: The hours become 1.
Split the miles evenly across the hours.
Compute the division.
State the speed with its label.

sentence_starters: The unit rate is ___ per 1 ___ because I divided ___ by ___.
I split ___ evenly across ___ units, so each unit gets ___.

skills.name: Graph a two-variable relationship from a table of values

prerequisite_skill.description: Turn the rows of an x-y table into ordered pairs, plot them in the first quadrant, and extend the pattern.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A table pairs 2 hours with 6 miles. What ordered pair does that row give, and how do you plot it?

skills.i_do_script: A table of two quantities is a list of points waiting to be plotted. Watch: a walker covers 3 miles each hour, so the table pairs hours 1, 2, 3, 4 with miles 3, 6, 9, 12. Each row becomes an ordered pair with hours first: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12). I plot each pair, across for hours and up for miles, and the points line up in a straight path. The table, the pairs, and the graph all show the same relationship, and the pattern in the rows tells me what the next point will be.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the coordinates when turning a row into a point
canonical_error.example: For the row hours = 2, miles = 6, plots (6, 2) by going across 6 and up 2
canonical_error.why: The student does not connect each quantity to its axis. Hours live on the horizontal axis and miles on the vertical axis, so the row gives (2, 6): across 2, up 6. Swapping the numbers plots a different relationship.

skills.item_template: A short x-y table from a real context with a constant additive pattern. Student writes ordered pairs, plots or names points, and extends the table. Short response; occasional MC.

sample_items.stem: A table pairs 2 hours with 6 miles. Hours go on the horizontal axis. Write the ordered pair for that row.
A table row shows hours = 4 and miles = 12. Which ordered pair matches that row?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (12, 4) swaps the coordinates; (4, 4) repeats the x-value; (12, 12) repeats the y-value. Hours are the across number, so the row gives (4, 12).

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 5, 10, 15. What y-value goes with x = 4?
To plot the point (3, 9), how far do you go across and how far up?
The points (1, 2), (2, 4), and (3, 6) are plotted. Do they lie on a straight line?
A table gives the cost y for x books: (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12). Write the next ordered pair.
A point is plotted 5 across and 10 up. Which table row does it show?
sample_items.distractor_logic: x = 10, y = 5 swaps across and up; the repeats ignore one of the two distances. Across gives x = 5 and up gives y = 10.

sample_items.stem: In the ordered pair (7, 2), which number is the x-value, the across number?

redirect_script.stop: Which quantity lives on the horizontal axis?
redirect_script.prompt: Label the axes first: the first column of the table goes across, the second goes up. Then each row reads in order, across then up. Touch the axis label as you say each number.
redirect_script.praise: You matched each number to its axis, so every row landed on the right point.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers that locate a point: the x-value (across) first, then the y-value (up).
One of the two number lines on a graph: the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis.

worked_example_script.text: Write the table: hours 1, 2, 3, 4 and miles 3, 6, 9, 12. Draw a first-quadrant grid with hours across and miles up.
What ordered pair does the first row give? Which number goes across?
Hours are the across number: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12). Plot each one, across then up. The points line up in a straight path because the miles grow by 3 every hour.
If a student plots (6, 2) for the 2-hour row, point at the axes: is 6 an hour amount or a mile amount? The hours axis only goes with the hours column.
Your turn: a table pairs 1, 2, 3 bags with 4, 8, 12 apples. Write the ordered pairs and plot them.

practice_problems.stem: A table row shows x = 3 and y = 7. Write the ordered pair.
To plot (2, 5), how far across and how far up do you go?
practice_problems.answer: 2 across, 5 up

practice_problems.stem: A table pairs weeks 1, 2, 3 with $20, $40, $60 saved. Write the three ordered pairs (weeks across).
A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 6, 12, 18, 24. What ordered pair comes next?
The points (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15) are plotted. Describe the path they make.
practice_problems.answer: They lie on a straight line; y goes up 5 each time x goes up 1.

practice_problems.stem: A row pairs 4 minutes with 8 laps. Minutes go across. Plot instructions?
practice_problems.answer: Go 4 across and 8 up, the point (4, 8).

practice_problems.stem: A table pairs x = 2, 4, 6 with y = 3, 6, 9. Write the ordered pair for x = 8 and explain how you know.
practice_problems.answer: (8, 12); y is always 1.5 times x (each step of 2 in x adds 3 to y).

practice_problems.stem: Nia plotted the row hours = 2, miles = 8. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Nia swapped the coordinates. Hours go across, so the row gives (2, 8): 2 across and 8 up.

activities.title: Table to Trail
activities.instructions:
1. Label the axes: hours across, miles up.
2. Read the first row aloud as an ordered pair: (1, 3).
3. Place a counter by walking a finger across 1 and up 3, then mark the point. Repeat for every row.
4. Lay a ruler along the counters: do they line up? Say why (miles grow by 3 every hour).
5. Predict where the 5-hour point will land, then check with the pattern.

activities.title: Row and Point Pairs
materials: Card deck: table-row cards and ordered-pair cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each table-row card, like weeks = 3, dollars = 60, to its ordered-pair card, like (3, 60).
3. To claim a match, say which number goes across and which goes up.
4. Two decoy cards swap the coordinates; set them aside and explain the swap.

strategy_links.why: Walking a finger across then up and placing counters makes the row-to-point translation physical before it is a convention.
The coordinate swap is a precise, common error; spotting it in plotted decoys names it cleanly.
Choral 'across first, then up' builds the automatic ordering the plotting convention depends on.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity goes on the horizontal axis, and where does the table tell you that?
What ordered pair does this row give? Say it as across, then up.
Do the plotted points line up? What in the table makes that happen?
Where will the next point land? How do you know before plotting it?
If we swapped the axes, what would happen to every point?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the coordinates when plotting a row.
misconception_redirects.say: Touch the axis labels: hours live on the across axis, so the hours number moves you across. Read the row again as across, then up.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched each number to its axis, so the point tells the truth about the row.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots points correctly but cannot extend the table.
misconception_redirects.say: Look at how y changes each time x goes up 1. Keep that same step going: what does the next row have to be?
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the pattern in the table to predict the next point, that is exactly how tables and graphs connect.

quick_checks.prompt: Write and plot the ordered pair for the row x = 3, y = 12.
A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 4, 8, 12. What pair comes next?
quick_checks.look_for: (4, 16), continuing the add-4 pattern in y as x steps by 1.

worked_solution.stem: A walker covers 3 miles each hour. The table pairs hours 1, 2, 3 with miles 3, 6, 9. Write the ordered pairs and describe the graph.
worked_solution.answer: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9); the points lie on a straight line

steps.annotation: Assign each quantity to its axis before writing pairs.
Each row becomes a pair with the hours number first.

steps.math: plot each pair: across, then up
steps.annotation: The across number comes from the hours column every time.
Miles grow by the same 3 every hour, so the path is straight.

faded_example.stem: A reader finishes 4 pages each minute. The table pairs minutes 1, 2, 3 with pages 4, 8, 12. Write the ordered pairs and describe the graph.
faded_example.answer: (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12); the points lie on a straight line

steps.annotation: Assign each quantity to its axis.
Turn each row into a pair, minutes first.
Tell how to plot the pair (2, 8): how far across and up?
Describe the shape the three points make and why.

sentence_starters: The row ___ becomes the point (___, ___) because ___ goes across.
The points line up because y changes by ___ every time x goes up 1.

skills.name: Define slope and identify the vertical and horizontal change
skills.i_do_script: Slope means vertical change for each unit of horizontal change -- how far up for how far across -- and the way to own that is to draw the ramp. A slope of 9/4: starting anywhere, go up 9 and across 4, and the line through those corners IS the ramp the fraction describes. The top number is the vertical change and the bottom is the horizontal, because slope answers 'how much UP per ACROSS.' Drawn on a grid, 9/4 is a steep ramp (more up than across) while 4/9 is a shallow one -- flipping the fraction changes the hill, which is why the positions matter.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps vertical and horizontal -- reads the top number as horizontal change and the bottom as vertical
canonical_error.example: For a slope of 9/4, says 9 is the horizontal change and 4 is the vertical change, reading the slope upside down
canonical_error.why: The student forgets that slope is vertical (up) over horizontal (across). The top of the fraction is always the vertical change; flipping it describes a different, steeper-or-flatter line.

skills.item_template: A slope given as a fraction. Student names which number is the vertical change and which is the horizontal change. Short response / dropdown.

sample_items.stem: The slope of a line is 9/4. What does the 9 represent?
The slope of a line is 9/4. What does the 4 represent?
Slope is defined as which change over which change?
A ramp has a slope of 3/5. Which number is the vertical change?
A line has a slope of 7/2. The 2 represents the ___ change.

redirect_script.stop: Which part of the slope is the UP part?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the ramp: from a dot, count up the top number and across the bottom, and look at the hill you made. Slope is vertical change OVER horizontal change: the top number is how far you go up (vertical), the bottom number is how far you go across (horizontal). Point to the top and say 'up'; the bottom, 'across.'
redirect_script.praise: You read the top as the vertical change and the bottom as the horizontal change -- that's what slope means.

vocabulary.definition: The vertical change for each unit of horizontal change on a line.
How far a line goes up (or down); the top number of a slope fraction.
How far a line goes across; the bottom number of a slope fraction.

worked_example_script.text: On a grid, start at (0, 0), count UP 9 and ACROSS 4, and mark the corner points of the ramp for slope 9/4.
Is this ramp steep or shallow? What ramp would 4/9 draw instead -- and why does swapping top and bottom change the hill?
Write 'The slope of a line is 5/2. What does each number represent?'
Which number is the up amount, and which is the across amount?
Slope is vertical over horizontal: the 5 on top is the vertical change (up 5), the 2 on the bottom is the horizontal change (across 2).
If a student says the 2 is the vertical change, ask 'which number is on top -- the up part or the across part?'
Your turn: for a slope of 8/3, name the vertical change and the horizontal change.

practice_problems.stem: Slope is defined as vertical change over what?
practice_problems.answer: Horizontal change

practice_problems.stem: In the slope 6/5, which number is the vertical change?
practice_problems.answer: 6 (the top number)

practice_problems.stem: The slope of a line is 9/4. What does the 9 represent, and what does the 4 represent?
practice_problems.answer: 9 is the vertical change (up 9); 4 is the horizontal change (across 4).
practice_problems.notes: Straight from the standard's definition; baits swapping the two.

practice_problems.stem: A road has a slope of 3/10. Describe the vertical and horizontal change in words.
practice_problems.answer: The road rises 3 (vertical change) for every 10 it moves across (horizontal change).
practice_problems.notes: Connect the fraction to 'up for every across.'

practice_problems.stem: Dana labeled the parts of a slope. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Dana wrote: 'The 7 is the horizontal change and the 2 is the vertical change.'
practice_problems.answer: Dana read the slope upside down. Slope is vertical change over horizontal change, so the top number 7 is the vertical change and the bottom number 2 is the horizontal change.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: swapping vertical and horizontal.

practice_problems.stem: A line has a slope of 2/9. Which number tells how far the line goes up per step across?
practice_problems.answer: The 2 (vertical change); the 9 is the horizontal change.
practice_problems.notes: Small-over-large slope so 'bigger number = up' guessing fails.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why a slope of 4/1 and a slope of 1/4 do NOT describe the same steepness.
practice_problems.answer: 4/1 goes up 4 for every 1 across (steep); 1/4 goes up 1 for every 4 across (nearly flat). The vertical and horizontal changes are swapped, so the lines are very different.
practice_problems.notes: Reverses direction: contrast the two orders.

practice_problems.stem: A line goes up 5 for every 8 it moves across. Write its slope, and name the vertical and horizontal change.
practice_problems.answer: Slope = 5/8; vertical change = 5, horizontal change = 8.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own: build the slope from a description.

activities.title: Draw the Ramp
activities.instructions:

skills.i_do_script: To decide if a table shows a constant or varying rate, I find how much y changes for each equal step of x. misconception_redirects.praise: You found the situation whose change differs each step -- that's a varying rate.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student can't decide because two situations both 'go up.'
misconception_redirects.say: Both totals go up, but check the AMOUNT added each step. Same amount = constant; different amount = varying.
misconception_redirects.praise: You compared the per-step amounts instead of just the direction.

quick_checks.prompt: Is 'a population grows 3% each year' constant or varying?
quick_checks.look_for: Varying. 'Constant' diagnoses treating a percent as a fixed amount.

quick_checks.prompt: Is 'a car travels 50 miles each hour' constant or varying?
quick_checks.look_for: Constant. 'Varying' means the student is confusing a changing total with a varying rate.

sentence_starters: This situation is varying because the amount of change is ___ each step.
The others are constant because they add ___ every time.

worked_solution.stem: Which situation has a varying rate of change: (a) a worker earns $18 each hour, (b) a bacteria count doubles each hour, (c) a candle burns 2 cm each hour, (d) a car travels 55 miles each hour?
worked_solution.answer: (b) a bacteria count doubles each hour

steps.annotation: $18, 2 cm, 55 miles -- same amount each step (constant).
Doubling multiplies, so the amount added grows.
That is what 'varying rate' means.
Only (b) has a varying rate of change.

faded_example.stem: Which situation has a varying rate of change: (a) a hiker climbs 100 feet each hour, (b) a printer prints 12 pages each minute, (c) an investment grows 6% each year, (d) a bus travels 40 miles each hour?

steps.annotation: Same amount each step -- constant.
A percent of a changing value.
Explain why (c)'s amount changes each year.
State which choice has a varying rate.

skills.name: Interpret the meaning of a slope value in a real-world context
skills.i_do_script: Draw the ramp before saying any words: from the ground go 9 across and only 2 up -- a long, gentle ramp. Now draw the flipped one, 2 across and 9 up: that's nearly a wall. Slope 2/9 can only be one of those two pictures, and the drawing decides which. To interpret a slope in context, I read the top number as the vertical rise and the bottom as the horizontal distance. Watch a ramp with slope 1/12: the top 1 is the vertical rise, the bottom 12 is the horizontal distance, so it means 'the ramp rises 1 foot for every 12 feet of horizontal distance.' The trap is saying 'rises 12 feet for every 1 foot' -- that flips the meaning.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the meaning -- states the horizontal number as the rise and the vertical number as the across distance
canonical_error.example: For a ramp with slope 1/12, says 'it rises 12 feet for every 1 foot across' instead of 'rises 1 foot for every 12 feet across'
canonical_error.why: The student flips vertical and horizontal when putting the slope into words. The top of the slope is the vertical rise; the bottom is the horizontal distance -- reversing them describes a far steeper ramp.

skills.item_template: A real-world slope given as a fraction (rise/run). Student selects/writes the correct 'rises __ for every __ across' interpretation. MC or short response.

sample_items.stem: A ramp has a slope of 1/12. What does this mean in context?
sample_items.answer: The ramp rises 1 foot for every 12 feet of horizontal distance.
choices: The ramp rises 1 foot for every 12 feet of horizontal distance.
The ramp rises 12 feet for every 1 foot of horizontal distance.
The ramp rises 1 foot for every 1 foot of horizontal distance.
The ramp rises 13 feet for every 12 feet of horizontal distance.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Slope 1/12 = rise 1 over run 12. Reversing gives 'rises 12 for every 1' (the classic error).

sample_items.stem: A road has a slope of 3/10 (rise over run). Interpret the slope in context.
sample_items.answer: The road rises 3 feet for every 10 feet of horizontal distance.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Top 3 is the rise, bottom 10 is the run.

sample_items.stem: A wheelchair ramp has a slope of 1/8. What does the slope mean?
sample_items.answer: The ramp rises 1 foot for every 8 feet of horizontal distance.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 up for every 8 across; reversing gives '8 up for every 1.'

sample_items.stem: A trail rises 2 feet for every 25 feet of horizontal distance. What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise 2 over run 25 = 2/25; writing 25/2 reverses rise and run.

redirect_script.stop: Which number is the UP and which is the ACROSS?
redirect_script.prompt: Look back at the two ramps on the grid -- the gentle one ends at (9, 2) and the wall ends at (2, 9). Which one did your sentence just describe? The top number of the slope is the vertical rise; the bottom is the horizontal distance. Read it as 'rises TOP for every BOTTOM across.' If you say 'rises 12 for every 1' on a slope of 1/12, you flipped it -- read the top as the rise.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the top number to the rise and the bottom to the across distance -- that's the correct interpretation.

vocabulary.definition: The vertical change of a slope -- the top number in rise over run.
The horizontal change of a slope -- the bottom number in rise over run.

worked_example_script.text: Plot the slope-2/9 ramp: start at (0, 0) and end 9 across, 2 up, at (9, 2). Then mark where the FLIPPED reading would end -- 2 across, 9 up, at (2, 9).
Which point ends a gentle wheelchair ramp, and which ends something close to a climbing wall? If a ramp 'rose 9 feet for every 2 across,' which point would it hit?
The gentle ramp rises 2 for every 9 across -- the top of 2/9 is the small UP move and the bottom is the long ACROSS move. Saying it backward describes the wall.
Write 'A ramp has a slope of 2/9. What does it mean?'
Which number is the rise (up), and which is the run (across)?
Top 2 is the rise, bottom 9 is the run: it rises 2 feet for every 9 feet across.
If a student says 'rises 9 for every 2,' ask 'which number is on top -- the rise or the run?'
Your turn: a ramp has slope 1/6. State what it means in context.

practice_problems.stem: In a slope of rise over run, which number is the vertical rise?
practice_problems.answer: The top number

practice_problems.stem: A ramp has slope 1/10. It rises how much for every 10 feet across?
practice_problems.answer: 1 foot

practice_problems.stem: A ramp has a slope of 1/12. Write what it means in context.
practice_problems.answer: It rises 1 foot for every 12 feet of horizontal distance.

practice_problems.stem: A road has a slope of 3/10. Write what it means in context.
practice_problems.answer: It rises 3 feet for every 10 feet of horizontal distance.

practice_problems.stem: Rosa interpreted a ramp's slope. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Rosa wrote: 'It rises 8 feet for every 1 foot of horizontal distance.'
practice_problems.answer: Rosa reversed the rise and run. Slope 1/8 means the ramp rises 1 foot (top) for every 8 feet (bottom) of horizontal distance -- a gentle ramp, not a steep one.

practice_problems.stem: A trail rises 2 feet for every 25 feet across. Write the slope.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction: from words to fraction.

practice_problems.stem: Two ramps: ramp A has slope 1/12, ramp B has slope 1/6. Which is steeper, and why?
practice_problems.answer: Ramp B (1/6) is steeper: it rises 1 foot for every 6 feet across, while ramp A rises 1 foot for every 12 feet. Less run for the same rise means steeper.

practice_problems.stem: A ramp is described as 'rising 1 foot for every 20 feet.' A builder writes the slope as 20/1. Explain the mistake and give the correct slope.
practice_problems.answer: The builder reversed rise and run. Rise is 1, run is 20, so the slope is 1/20, not 20/1. 20/1 would be an extremely steep ramp.
practice_problems.notes: Diagnose a reversed slope from a description.

activities.title: Slope to Meaning
materials: Card set: 6 slope fractions and 8 'rises __ for every __' meaning cards (two reversed decoys)
activities.instructions:

2. To claim a match, point to the top number as the rise and the bottom as the run.
3. Two meaning cards have the rise and run reversed -- set them aside and explain the flip.
4. Debrief: how can you catch a reversed interpretation quickly?

activities.title: Reversed Ramp
activities.instructions:
1. Read Rosa's claim that slope 1/8 means 'rises 8 feet for every 1 foot.'
2. Circle the top number and label it 'rise'; circle the bottom and label it 'run.'
3. Rewrite the correct meaning.
4. Write one sentence on why the reversed ramp would be far steeper.

content.worked_problem: Ramp slope 1/8. Rosa wrote 'rises 8 feet for every 1 foot.'
content.error_step: Rosa reversed the rise and the run.
content.why: Slope 1/8 means rise 1 (top) over run 8 (bottom): rises 1 foot for every 8 feet across.

strategy_links.why: Drawing the rise and run of a slope on a grid grounds the 'rises __ for every __' interpretation.
The reversed-rise-and-run interpretation is a precise error a find-and-fix names cleanly.
Thinking aloud 'top is the rise, bottom is the run' models the correct read every time.

Read it as 'rises ___ for every ___ across.'
If you flip the two numbers, is the ramp steeper or gentler?
Does your sentence match the top-over-bottom order?
Which slope would be the steepest ramp?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student states the run as the rise and the rise as the run (reversed interpretation).
misconception_redirects.say: The top number of the slope is the vertical rise; the bottom is the horizontal distance. Read it as 'rises TOP for every BOTTOM across.' If you say 'rises 12 for every 1' on a slope of 1/12, you flipped it -- read the top as the rise.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the top number to the rise and the bottom to the across distance -- that's the correct interpretation.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the numbers ('rises 13 for every 12') instead of reading them as rise and run.
misconception_redirects.say: Slope is not a sum -- it's rise over run. Keep the top as the rise and the bottom as the run; don't add them.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the rise and run separate instead of adding them.

quick_checks.look_for: Rises 1 foot for every 10 feet across. 'Rises 10 for every 1' diagnoses the reversed error.

quick_checks.prompt: A path rises 3 feet for every 4 feet across. What is the slope?
quick_checks.look_for: 3/4. An answer of 4/3 means rise and run were reversed.

sentence_starters: The top number ___ is the rise and the bottom ___ is the run, so it rises ___ for every ___ across.
Slope ___ means for every ___ feet across, it rises ___ feet.

worked_solution.stem: A ramp has a slope of 2/9. Interpret the slope in context.
worked_solution.answer: The ramp rises 2 feet for every 9 feet of horizontal distance.

steps.annotation: Slope is vertical rise over horizontal run.
The top number is the vertical rise.
The bottom number is the horizontal distance.

steps.math: rises 2 ft for every 9 ft across

faded_example.stem: A road has a slope of 3/20. Interpret the slope in context.
faded_example.answer: The road rises 3 feet for every 20 feet of horizontal distance.

skills.name: Analyze and compare rates of change in a table to justify linearity
skills.i_do_script: When a table's rate changes partway through, I find the rate for each part separately -- change in y over change in x -- and compare. Watch a balance: months 0,1,2 give 10, 18, 26 (up 8 each), then months 2,3,4,5 give 26, 29, 32, 35 (up 3 each). The first part's rate is 8 per month; the second is 3 per month. Because the rates differ, one linear function cannot model the whole table.

canonical_error.pattern: Computes one rate across the whole span and calls the table a single linear function, missing that the segment rates differ
canonical_error.example: For a table going 10, 18, 26, 29, 32, 35 over months 0-5, computes (35 - 10)/(5 - 0) = 5 and calls it one linear function, ignoring that the parts rise by 8 then 3
canonical_error.why: Averaging over the whole span hides a change in rate. A single linear function requires the SAME rate on every interval; the student must check segments, not just endpoints.

skills.item_template: A table whose rate shifts partway (piecewise). Part A: find a segment's rate of change. Part B: explain why one linear function can't model it. Multi-part.

sample_items.stem: The table shows a bank balance over months. Part A: What is the rate of change from Month 0 to Month 2? Part B: Can one linear function model the whole table? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Part A: 8 dollars per month [(26 - 10)/(2 - 0)]. Part B: No -- from Month 2 to 5 the rate is 3 dollars per month [(35 - 26)/(5 - 2)], and 8 does not equal 3, so a single linear function cannot model it.

sample_items.stem: The table shows distance over hours. Part A: What is the rate of change from Hour 0 to Hour 2? Part B: Can one linear function model the whole table? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Part A: 5 miles per hour [(10 - 0)/(2 - 0)]. Part B: No -- from Hour 2 to 5 the rate is 8 miles per hour [(34 - 10)/(5 - 2)], so the rate changes and one linear function cannot model it.

sample_items.stem: A table's items produced go 4, 7, 10, 16, 22 for days 0 through 4. Find the rate for Day 0 to Day 2, and the rate for Day 2 to Day 4.
sample_items.answer: Day 0-2: 3 items per day [(10 - 4)/2]. Day 2-4: 6 items per day [(22 - 10)/2].

sample_items.stem: A table rises by 6 each hour for the first 3 hours, then by 6 each hour for the next 3 hours. Can one linear function model it? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes -- both segments rise by the same rate (6 per hour), so the rate is constant the whole time and one linear function models it.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Equal segment rates means it IS one linear function -- the contrast case.

redirect_script.stop: Did the rate stay the same the WHOLE table?
redirect_script.prompt: Find the rate for each segment separately -- change in y over change in x for that part. If two segments give different rates, one linear function can't model it. Don't average over the whole span; compare the segment rates.
redirect_script.praise: You found each segment's rate and compared them -- that's how you prove it isn't one linear function.

vocabulary.definition: A part of the table between two points where you compute a single rate of change.
Change in y divided by change in x over a chosen part of the table.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.AF.3 and 8.AF.4 (graph linear functions and compare rates of change).

worked_example_script.text: Write a table: Month 0,1,2,3,4,5 with Balance 6, 14, 22, 27, 32, 37.
What's the rate from Month 0 to 2? From Month 2 to 5?
0 to 2: (22 - 6)/(2 - 0) = 8 per month. 2 to 5: (37 - 22)/(5 - 2) = 5 per month. Different rates, so not one linear function.
If a student does (37 - 6)/5 = 6.2 and says 'linear,' ask 'did the rate stay the same the whole time, or did it change partway?'
Your turn: find each segment's rate for Balance 5, 10, 15, 24, 33 over months 0-4.

practice_problems.stem: From Month 0 to Month 2, y goes from 10 to 26. What is the rate of change?
practice_problems.answer: 8 per month [(26 - 10)/2]

practice_problems.stem: If one part of a table rises 8 per step and another rises 3 per step, is it one linear function?
practice_problems.answer: No -- the rates differ.

practice_problems.stem: A balance goes 10, 18, 26, 29, 32, 35 over months 0-5. Find the rate from Month 0 to 2.
practice_problems.answer: 8 dollars per month [(26 - 10)/(2 - 0)].

practice_problems.stem: For the same table (10, 18, 26, 29, 32, 35, months 0-5), can one linear function model it? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- Month 0-2 rises 8 per month, but Month 2-5 rises 3 per month [(35 - 26)/3], so the rate changes.

practice_problems.stem: Nora analyzed a table. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Nora wrote: '(22 - 4)/(4 - 0) = 4.5, so it's one linear function with rate 4.5.'
practice_problems.answer: Nora averaged over the whole span. Check segments: x 0-2 rises 3 per step [(10 - 4)/2], x 2-4 rises 6 per step [(22 - 10)/2]. The rates differ, so it is NOT one linear function.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: whole-span average hides the rate change.

practice_problems.stem: A table's distance goes 0, 5, 10, 18, 26, 34 over hours 0-5. Find the rate from Hour 2 to Hour 5.
practice_problems.answer: 8 miles per hour [(34 - 10)/(5 - 2)].

practice_problems.stem: A table rises 6 per hour for the first 3 hours, then 6 per hour for the next 3. Can one linear function model it? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- both segments have the same rate (6 per hour), so the rate is constant throughout and one linear function fits.
practice_problems.notes: Contrast case: equal segment rates ARE linear.

practice_problems.stem: Create a 5-row table whose rate changes partway through, and explain how you know one linear function can't model it.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (0,0),(1,2),(2,4),(3,9),(4,14). First part rises 2 per step, second part rises 5 per step. Because the segment rates differ (2 vs 5), no single linear function fits.

activities.title: Don't Average the Whole Thing
activities.instructions:
1. Read Nora's claim that y = 4, 7, 10, 16, 22 is one linear function with rate 4.5.
2. Compute the rate for x 0 to 2, then for x 2 to 4, separately.
3. Decide whether one linear function fits, and explain using both segment rates.
4. Debrief: why can the whole-span rate hide a change in rate?

content.worked_problem: Table y = 4, 7, 10, 16, 22 for x = 0-4. Nora wrote '(22-4)/4 = 4.5, so linear.'
content.error_step: Nora used a single whole-span average instead of checking each segment.
content.why: x 0-2 rises 3 per step and x 2-4 rises 6 per step -- different rates, so not one linear function.

activities.title: One Line or Two?
materials: Card set of 8 short tables (some constant throughout, some piecewise)
activities.instructions:
1. For each table, compute the rate for the first half and the second half.
2. Sort into 'One linear function (rates match)' and 'Not one linear function (rates differ).'
3. For each 'not one' card, write the two different rates.
4. Debrief: what has to be true for one linear function to model the whole table?

strategy_links.why: A written justification of why the rates differ builds the explain-and-support skill the summative item demands.
The whole-span-average error is precise; a find-and-fix that checks each segment corrects it.
Comparing a truly linear table to a piecewise one makes the 'same rate on every interval' criterion explicit.
Think-pair-share on 'can one line fit this?' rehearses the justification aloud before writing.

questioning_prompts: What is the rate for the first part? For the second part?
Are those two rates the same or different?
Did you check segments, or average the whole table?
If the rates differ, can one linear function model it?
How would you word your justification using the rates?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes one rate across the whole span and calls the table one linear function.
misconception_redirects.say: Find the rate for each segment separately -- change in y over change in x for that part. If two segments give different rates, one linear function can't model it. Don't average over the whole span; compare the segment rates.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found each segment's rate and compared them -- that's how you prove it isn't one linear function.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds the segment rates but forgets to state a conclusion.
misconception_redirects.say: Now compare: are the rates equal? Then say clearly whether one linear function can model it and why.
misconception_redirects.praise: You compared the segment rates and stated a clear conclusion -- that's a complete justification.

quick_checks.prompt: A table rises 4 per step for x 0-2 and 4 per step for x 2-4. One linear function?
quick_checks.look_for: Yes -- rates match (4 and 4). 'No' means the student mis-computed a segment.

quick_checks.prompt: A table goes 0, 6, 12, 15, 18 (x steps by 1). Find the two segment rates.
quick_checks.look_for: 6 per step then 3 per step. A single rate of 4.5 diagnoses the whole-span-average error.

Because the rates are ___, the table ___ be modeled by a single linear function.

worked_solution.answer: Part A: 8 dollars per month. Part B: No -- the rate changes from 8 to 3 per month.

Do the same for the second segment.
The two segment rates are different.
One linear function needs the same rate on every interval.

faded_example.answer: Part A: 5 miles per hour. Part B: No -- the rate changes from 5 to 8 per hour.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5, interpreting a slope in a real context, the At-proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, move up to S6, analyzing a table whose rate shifts and justifying why one linear function cannot model it. If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks whether they can find a unit rate at all, and B2 checks whether they can turn a table into plotted points, the two grade 6 skills slope and constant-rate work lean on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (first-quadrant plotting) and F2 (equal-groups multiplication and division) locate the gap in grades 3 to 5. S1 through S4 remain available to probe the standard's own definition, table classification, and situation-sorting work.
